REP: Marcus, I appreciate the time. I'd like to understand your business a bit before I show you anything. Is it all right if I ask a few questions first?
CUSTOMER: Go for it. Just know I've heard a lot of pitches this month.
REP: Fair enough. What's changed most in your business over the last year?
CUSTOMER: Reimbursement, mostly. The PBMs keep squeezing us. I'm filling more prescriptions than ever and making less on each one. I've had to cut a tech's hours. Three years ago I had four techs. Now I have three, and one of them is part-time.
REP: That's tough. Where are you looking to make it up?
CUSTOMER: Anything that isn't dispensing. Vaccines have been good to us, so I've been thinking about other clinical services. I just haven't found one that fits. I looked at diabetes education, but the billing was a nightmare, and I looked at travel vaccines, but there isn't enough demand out here.
REP: How do you decide whether a new service is worth it?
CUSTOMER: Simple. It has to pay for the staff time inside a month or two, and it can't mess up my workflow at the counter. Everything I add gets judged against those two rules.
REP: Makes sense. When you think about your counter on a busy day, what usually breaks first?
CUSTOMER: Phones. When the phones back up, everything backs up. One tech on the phone, one at the register, and I'm checking scripts as fast as I can. Tuesday and Wednesday afternoons are the worst, because that's when the doctors' offices send everything over at once.
REP: Thanks, that helps. Here's why I think RapidPanel fits your two rules. Each test takes about five minutes of staff time across the swab and the documentation, the kits cost about twelve dollars, and stores like yours charge thirty-five to forty in cash. So one test pays for about an hour of tech time.
CUSTOMER: On paper. But who's going to pay forty dollars cash? My customers are price-sensitive. They'll go to urgent care, where their insurance covers it.
REP: That's a real concern, and I'd rather test it than assume. When someone with a sore throat goes to urgent care around here, how long do they usually wait?
CUSTOMER: The one on Route 9? Two, three hours on a weekend. People complain about it all the time. I hear about it every Monday when they come in with their prescriptions.
REP: And what's their copay there, typically?
CUSTOMER: Depends on the plan. Seventy-five, a hundred dollars for a lot of people with high-deductible plans. Most of the families around here switched to those plans when the plant changed insurers last year.
REP: So for a lot of your customers the choice isn't forty dollars versus free. It's forty dollars and ten minutes here, versus a seventy-five-dollar copay and a three-hour wait. Our stores in similar towns see about sixty percent of parents choose the cash test once they hear that. Does that change how you see the cash price?
CUSTOMER: When you put it that way, yeah. The high-deductible people would go for it. And the parents who work hourly would pay just to not lose the afternoon.
REP: Good. What else would stop you from moving forward?
CUSTOMER: The minimum order. I don't want fifty kits expiring in my fridge.
REP: Understood. The kits are stored at room temperature, not in the fridge, and they're good for eighteen months. Even at three tests a week, fifty kits last you about four months, well inside the date. And once a year we swap any kit that's within ninety days of expiring. Does that address the expiry worry?
CUSTOMER: Room temperature helps. Okay, that addresses it.
REP: Then here's the next step I'd propose. I'll send you the agreement and a one-page break-even based on three tests a week today. Then let's meet next Tuesday, the 22nd, at 1:30, after your lunch rush, to sign the CLIA packet and pick a training date. Does that work?
CUSTOMER: Tuesday the 22nd at 1:30 works. Send the break-even first, though. I want to run my own numbers.
REP: Absolutely. You'll have it within the hour.
CUSTOMER: All right, Daniel. Talk Tuesday.
